item.title: Inner speech and thinking
item.description:
Many of us talk to ourselves silently as we read, plan, or work through a tricky problem, while others think mostly in images, feelings, or wordless concepts. We study what triggers inner speech, what forms it takes – from a single silent word to a full internal conversation – and how it shapes what we perceive and do next.

Our research is guided by Linguistic Active Inference Theory (Yao, 2025, Psychological Review), which proposes that inner speech helps the mind and body manage uncertainty. When a situation is unclear, putting thoughts into words specifies what we expect to see or hear and helps turn broad goals into coordinated physical actions. Because inner speech adapts to the problem at hand, the same framework connects its everyday uses – such as silent reading, planning, and self-awareness – with the striking differences in how often people experience an inner voice.

Looking ahead, we combine controlled experiments, naturalistic problem solving, and self-talking computational models to trace how inner speech unfolds in real time. By pairing brain recordings (EEG) with ultrasound imaging of tiny tongue movements and eye tracking, we are also developing objective ways to detect spontaneous inner speech as it happens. Curious about your own inner voice? Try our 3-minute inner-voice self-test.

item.title: Embodied and situated language
item.description:
Words do not carry fixed dictionary meanings. What a word means – and how it shapes what we feel or do – shifts with our bodies, senses, emotions, and cultural surroundings. We study how that grounding works for concrete objects and for abstract ideas such as trust or love. Our research shows that size acts as a core organising principle across concepts – much like the familiar idea that “size matters”, it helps set the scale and intensity of our judgements and actions – while emotion, imagery, and culture shape how words are understood across first and second languages.

The same embodied process operates when we direct language at ourselves in inner speech, linking silent words with movement and perception – and raising sharp questions about how human understanding differs from AI language models. We study meaning-making in real-world settings such as reading and classrooms. Using eye tracking to see how readers sample upcoming words in context, we study how the mind predicts meaning on the fly and build adaptive digital text displays that respond smoothly to a reader’s gaze.

item.title: Voice hearing and rumination
item.description:
Some people hear voices that others around them do not – an occasional, harmless experience for many, and a persistent, distressing one for others. Many people also find themselves caught in loops of repetitive negative inner speech, known as rumination. We study both experiences as shifts in how inner speech, sensory expectations, and the body work together, asking when those shifts remain benign and when they become unhelpful or distressing.

Using listening experiments, brain recordings (EEG), and computational models of perception, we investigate how strong expectations can shape what a person hears in ambiguous sound. Alongside this, we are developing wearable methods that combine EEG and ultrasound imaging of tongue movements to detect ruminative inner speech and voice-hearing activity objectively. A central future question for our lab is whether these experiences share common mechanisms in how the mind regulates uncertainty and builds the ongoing story we tell ourselves.
